findings.statement: The bank is a financial entity to which DORA applies, being a credit institution listed in Annex I of DORA.
The external cloud provider is an ICT third-party service provider for the bank under DORA, and the hosted online banking systems support critical or important functions.
The bank must classify the incident as major or not major against the qualitative and quantitative thresholds it is required to define, and must record the incident in its ICT incident records.

Several hours of unavailability of customer-facing online banking can satisfy the definition of a major ICT-related incident, and where the bank so classifies it, the bank must report it to its competent authority, with an initial report within 4 hours after classification and no later than 24 hours after becoming aware, followed by intermediate and final reports under the deadlines in Article 18(3).

The bank must maintain and periodically test a business continuity policy and an incident response and recovery plan that ensure the continuity and recovery of the online banking services it has contracted to the cloud provider.

In relying on the cloud provider, the bank must apply a risk-based approach to ICT third-party risk and ensure its contract with the provider includes DORA's required terms, including access to, restoration and availability of data and the provider's obligations in case of business continuity failures or ICT-related incidents.

The bank must ensure it is able to access, restore and subsequently use all customer data held by the cloud provider, and must maintain a documented exit strategy for terminating the cloud arrangement.
The bank must keep and update its Register of Information covering the cloud arrangement as an ICT service supporting critical or important functions.

The cloud provider processes the bank's customer data as a processor, so the bank must use only a processor providing sufficient guarantees and must have the Article 28(3) contract stipulations in place, including the provider taking all measures required by Article 32.

The bank must ensure its security measures for the customer data on the disrupted systems include the ability to ensure the ongoing availability and resilience of the processing systems and the ability to restore the availability of and access to the personal data in a timely manner in the event of the technical incident.

The bank must assess whether the failure constitutes a personal data breach; where it does, the bank must notify it to its competent supervisory authority without undue delay and, where feasible, not later than 72 hours after becoming aware, unless it is unlikely to result in a risk, and must document any personal data breach.
Where the incident is likely to result in a high risk to customers' rights and freedoms, the bank must communicate the personal data breach to the affected customers without undue delay.

On the facts described, the bank is neither a provider nor a deployer of an AI system and no AI system is placed on the market or put into service, so the AI Act's obligations are not engaged in this scenario.

summaries.relevance: Defines the roles and uses to which the AI Act's obligations attach, allowing the conclusion that none of those roles is present on the scenario's facts.
Supplies the definition of an AI system against which the scenario's described systems are measured, supporting the conclusion that the AI Act is not engaged.
Lists credit institutions as financial entities, anchoring DORA's applicability to the bank across the incident, third-party and continuity findings.
Defines the provider-side category into which the external cloud host falls, framing the bank's third-party risk duties.
Supplies the definition on which the bank's classification of the outage as a major ICT-related incident turns, gating the Article 18 reporting duty.
Supplies the definition that determines whether the hosted online banking services count as critical or important functions, which conditions several of the bank's DORA duties.
Defines financial entity by reference to Annex I, completing the basis on which DORA applies to the bank.
Sets the risk-based approach the bank must follow in managing its reliance on the cloud provider.
Obliges the bank to include the key contract terms with the provider, notably data access and the provider's business-continuity and incident obligations, which are the crux of the reliance question.
Requires the bank to be able to access, restore and use the data held by the provider, directly addressing recovery of customer data after the failure.
Requires a documented exit strategy for the cloud arrangement, part of managing the reliance that failed during the incident.
Requires the bank to record the incident and significant disruptions, supporting the record-keeping conclusion.
Requires the bank to define and adhere to thresholds classifying incidents as major, the step that triggers or excludes the Article 18 reporting duty.
Establishes the duty to report major ICT-related incidents to the competent authority, the central DORA obligation for the incident.
Fixes the 4-hour and 24-hour deadlines for the initial report and the follow-up reporting rhythm the bank must meet once the incident is classified as major.
Requires the business continuity policy and incident response and recovery plan the bank must have maintained and operated for the outage.
Extends continuity and recovery planning expressly to functions contracted to ICT third-party providers such as the cloud host.
Requires yearly testing of continuity and recovery plans, a standing resilience duty relevant to the failure's recurrence.
Requires the register of information documenting the cloud arrangement, part of the bank's structured reliance on the provider.
Supplies the definition of personal data breach against which the bank must measure the outage before any Article 33 duty arises.
Restricts the bank to processors giving sufficient guarantees, governing its use of the cloud provider for customer data.
Requires the processing contract to stipulate the provider's Article 32 security measures, tying the data protection contract terms to the failure.
Obliges the bank to ensure ongoing availability and resilience of the processing systems, the security dimension of the outage.
Obliges the bank to be able to restore the availability of and access to customer data in a timely manner after a technical incident, the most direct GDPR response to the failure.
Sets the 72-hour supervisory-authority notification duty that applies if the outage amounts to a personal data breach.
Requires documentation of any personal data breach, the record-keeping consequence for the incident.
Sets the duty to communicate the breach to affected customers where it is likely to result in high risk.

actions: Confirm whether the bank classified the incident as a major ICT-related incident under the thresholds required by DORA Article 17(4), since the reporting duty and deadlines turn on that classification.

Establish when the bank became aware of the failure and of any classification as major, to assess compliance with the Article 18(3) initial-report deadlines of 4 hours after classification and 24 hours after awareness.

Determine whether the outage involved destruction, loss, alteration of, or unauthorised disclosure of or access to customer personal data, since GDPR Article 33 notification and Article 34 communication depend on that characterisation.

Review the bank-cloud provider contract for the terms required by DORA Article 11(4) and the stipulations required by GDPR Article 28(3), including data access, restoration and provider obligations on incidents.
Verify whether the hosted online banking services constitute critical or important functions under DORA Article 3(1)(18) in the bank's actual operations, as several DORA duties depend on that status.
